beats.narration_text: Konnichiwa — this is Liam, in for Bear. Watch: I ask the AI about MY trek, and it hands me EVERYONE's trek. It knows the world. It does not know my world. That is the gap this film closes: how to teach it YOUR world, so it answers from your material, not the internet's.

beats.narration_text: The AI is smart when you give it your material. Upload your own documents — your notes, your team's manuals, your policies — and it stops answering from the internet and starts answering from your world. This film shows you what to hand it, the three habits that make it stick, and where the trick bites back.

beats.narration_text: Four terms. A knowledge base: your own documents, gathered in one place for the AI. An upload: copying a file into the chat so the AI can read it. Grounding: answering only from the material you handed it. And RAG: the AI searches your documents, then answers from what it finds. Plain words from here on.

beats.narration_text: Here is the problem. The AI trained on the internet — it knows everyone's everything, and nobody's specifics. Ask it who is on call Friday, and it has no rota to read, so it does what a confident stranger does: it guesses. A fluent, plausible, completely invented answer. The knowledge it needs exists — it just is not in its world. It is in yours — your docs: your files, your folders, your head.

beats.narration_text: The fix is embarrassingly simple: give it the source. Attach the rota, the manual, the notes — the file goes into the chat, and suddenly the answer has somewhere to come from. Most AI apps let you attach files to a conversation, including Claude's. And some give the project a permanent shelf: Claude's projects keep your documents on hand, so every chat in that project starts already knowing them.

beats.narration_text: What happens next is the clever part, and it has a name you will meet: RAG. The AI does not read all your documents — that would take forever. It searches them like a librarian, pulls only the matching pages — the rota, not the handbook — and reads those before it answers. Anthropic's own help pages describe exactly this: a search tool that retrieves only the most relevant information from your uploaded documents. Librarian, not scanner.

beats.narration_text: How does the librarian know which pages match? Every word becomes a point on a map — this is the 'embeddings' idea, in plain words. Points for similar meanings sit near each other: invoice, receipt, bill cluster together; elephant lands across the map. So when you ask about billing, the search pulls the invoice cluster, not the elephant. Meaning becomes distance. That is the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: So what belongs in the box? Three kinds of material. Your notes — the stuff in your head that the internet never saw. Your work documents — the handbook, the rota, the meeting notes your team actually lives by: your work docs. And the only-you-know pile — your data, your drafts, your sources. Rule of thumb: if you would attach it to an email to brief a new colleague, it belongs in the AI's world too.

beats.narration_text: Three habits make it stick. One: give it the source — attach the file, or keep it on the project's shelf. Two: pin it down — say 'answer only from these files,' and name the document, so it searches the rota instead of the handbook. Three: make it quote — ask for the exact line it used, and check the quote against your file. A citation you can verify beats a confident paragraph every time.

beats.narration_text: Now the teardown — where this bites. First, the AI never warns you about what is missing — your blind spots. It answers from what it has; silence is not disagreement. Second, stale documents give stale answers — the box needs weeding, or last year's policy becomes this year's confidently wrong reply. Third, it trusts your uploads completely. A wrong document does not get flagged; it gets quoted. Garbage in, confident garbage out.

beats.narration_text: The verdict. The AI answers from the world's knowledge — not yours. Hand it your documents and it searches them, reads the matching parts, and answers from your material. Pin it to the source, and make it quote. And the falsifiable test: ask about something only your files know. A generic answer means the upload never happened.

beats.narration_text: "Here is our on-call rota for this month: [paste it]. From now on, answer my scheduling questions only from this rota, and quote the line you used. First question: who is on call this Friday?" Pick any document only you have — a rota, a menu, a reading list. Paste it in, pin the AI to it, and ask a question whose answer you can check. Then check two things yourself: does the quote match your document, word for word? And what does it say when the answer is not in there? Take this prompt, run it on your own material — and see what it quotes.
